newsitem.title: FRANCE: EU Commission proposes new maximum work hours law.
newsitem.headline: EU Commission proposes new maximum work hours law.

text.p: European Union rules on working hours and rest times should also apply to workers they do not currently protect, the European Commission said on Tuesday.

"The exclusion of certain categories of workers from the general protection provided by the (EU's Working Time) Directive is an anomaly which needs to be corrected," European Social Affairs Commissioner Padraig Flynn said in a statement.

In a discussion paper on which EU governments, management and labour groups will be asked to comment by November, the Commission said "non-mobile" transport workers and sea fishermen should all be covered by the directive.
This guarantees them a maximum 48-hour week, night shifts of an average of eight hours, four weeks paid leave a year and at least one day off a week.
"Mobile" and people in the offshore oil industry, whose work patterns do not follow a normal working week, should be guaranteed the same annual leave and night shift limits.
But their rest periods and maximum working hours should be calculated on a yearly basis, the Commission white paper says.

The existing Working Time Directive, which was unsuccessfully challenged in court last year by Britain's former Conservative government, excludes about 5.6 million EU workers, some 3.5 million of them in the transport sector.
If the Commission has its way, the directive will also apply to doctors in training, who work notoriously long hours.
Britain has so far resisted including this group of workers.

This is partly because it wants to be able to carry out domestic health service reforms at its own pace, partly because London fears it would have to make cuts in hours which other member states would avoid, one British diplomat told Reuters.
The directive applies to employees, as British doctors are classed, but not self-employed workers, as trainee doctors are considered in most other EU countries.

While the white paper insists doctors in most countries are "employees for the purpose of employment law", the British diplomat said this did not necessarily mean they would be classed as employees for the purpose of the work hour rules.
This question is likely to be one of the main points of discussion when EU social affairs ministers discuss the white paper on October 7.

One possible solution mooted by the Comission -- which the diplomat said London could accept -- would be to set a 48-hour week for trainee doctors but let individual countries decide how many more hours they would have to stay on call.
A spokeswoman for Flynn said the Commission thought British doctors should have the same protection as other EU colleagues.
"Other member states seem to be able to maintain their health system without excluding junior doctors (from the work hour rules)," spokeswoman Barbara Nolan told Reuters.
